To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

low intake of folate, but not vitamins B6 or B12, at baseline was associated with an increased risk of incident mild cognitive impairment (or probable dementia) among postmenopausal women enrolled in the WHI.
higher intake of folate, but not vitamins B6 or B12, was associated with increased, and higher intake of vitamin B6 was associated with decreased, risk for MCI and probable dementia.
higher folate, vitamin b 6, and b 12 intake was associated with lower risk for mild cognitive impairment (mci) and probable dementia in later life.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the relationship between B vitamins and the development of dementia.
the role that B vitamins may play in preventing dementia.
the relationship between dietary intake of B vitamins and cognitive decline.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are no data to suggest that vitamin supplementation is effective in the prevention of dementia or cognitive impairment.

there is no evidence that vitamin B 6 or vitamin B 12 supplementation has any effect on cognitive function or on the risk of dementia, although the possibility that vitamin B 12 may be beneficial cannot be excluded.
the evidence is insufficient to support or refute an association between B vitamin intake and risk of MCI and/or dementia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have found a significant association between low folate intake and increased risk of MCI and dementia in a population of older women.

we found that folate intake below the recommended daily allowance may increase the risk of mild cognitive impairment/probable dementia in older women, but we found no significant associations between B6 or B12 and MCI/dementia.
the higher the intake of folate, the greater the risk of cognitive decline and dementia.

we found a significant association between lower levels of folate intake and an increased risk of developing MCI or probable dementia.
